Abstract This paper develops an integrative theoretical model explaining how and when AI-supported cybersecurity governance may contribute to organizational resilience. Using a theory-synthesis design and an integrative literature review, it connects scholarship on organizational resilience, cybersecurity governance, artificial intelligence governance, human-AI decision-making, adversarial machine learning, risk governance, organizational learning, and dynamic capabilities. AI-supported cybersecurity governance is conceptualized as a formal organizational arrangement through which heterogeneous AI-generated evidence–including predictive scores, anomaly signals, generative summaries, and semi-autonomous recommendations—is institutionally translated into cybersecurity direction, oversight, prioritization, coordination, reporting, accountability, and learning. The model identifies an AI-specific positive pathway: continuous processing at scale, heterogeneous-data fusion, nonlinear and cross-system pattern detection, probabilistic forecasting, rapid updating, and automated synthesis may create incremental governance value beyond periodic rule-based business intelligence or exclusively human analysis. These affordances are converted into organizational resilience through five governance mechanisms: enhanced visibility, improved prioritization, stronger coordination, more informed oversight, and structured organizational learning. Dynamic capabilities explain how these mechanisms support sensing, seizing, and reconfiguring, while organizational resilience is represented through anticipation, coping, and adaptation. The same pathway may be weakened or reversed by automation bias, model opacity, adversarial manipulation, vendor opacity, false prioritization, data-quality failure, and accountability gaps. The paper makes three contributions. First, it defines AI-supported cybersecurity governance as a distinct organizational construct and separates it from conventional cybersecurity governance, cybersecurity maturity, firm-wide AI capability, and isolated operational AI use. Second, it explains what AI changes in the positive pathway while explicitly recognizing heterogeneity across model classes and deployment arrangements. Third, it specifies external scope conditions, internal boundary conditions, and failure modes that make the proposed relationships testable and non-deterministic.
topics: Supply Chain Resilience and Risk Management

documents.abstract: Forensic identification has experienced a profound transformation with the advent of molecular biology techniques, shifting from traditional morphological and serological methods to highly sensitive and specific DNA-based approaches. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the evolution of molecular techniques in forensic science, beginning with conventional DNA profiling methods such as Restriction Fragment Length Polymorphism (RFLP) and Short Tandem Repeat (STR) analysis, and extending to advanced methodologies including mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) analysis, Y-chromosome markers, and Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS). The review critically examines the principles, applications, advantages, and limitations of these techniques in diverse forensic contexts, including crime scene investigation, human identification, kinship analysis, and mass disaster victim identification. Furthermore, it highlights recent advancements in forensic genomics, epigenetics, and microbiome-based approaches, along with the growing role of bioinformatics and artificial intelligence in data interpretation. Despite significant progress, challenges such as data complexity, ethical considerations, and the need for global standardization remain key concerns. Overall, this review underscores the pivotal role of molecular techniques in modern forensic science and emphasizes their continued evolution toward more precise, rapid, and comprehensive identification systems.

The development of multifunctional smart coatings for corrosion resistance and energy-based applications has been highly boosted owing to the fast development of materials science and artificial intelligence. The conventional approach used in mitigating corrosion has mainly been empirical and trial and error, which may prove to be inefficient at times. Conversely, artificial intelligence (AI)-based methods have proved useful in developing predictive models and optimising the performance of the coatings. This review focuses on the current advancements made in AI-aided design strategies that combine machine learning and deep learning techniques. In particular, attention is devoted to the consideration of multipurpose, such as polymer-nanocomposites, coatings-reinforced by MXenes, and multipurpose materials for applications in both corrosion protection and energy systems. Synergistic combination of machine learning and experimental verification, which includes electrochemical experiments and surface characterisation, is also considered for establishing reliable structure-property correlation. Additionally, hybrid modelling using AI in combination with statistical analysis and density functional theory (DFT) is also mentioned. Despite many achievements, there are still problems associated with the availability of data, interpretability of the models used, and generalisability to other materials. This review aims to critically summarise recent advances in AI-driven multifunctional smart coatings while highlighting future research directions, including closed-loop optimisation, digital twins, self-driving research platforms, and advanced smart coatings.

This study examined the influence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) on academic stress reduction as perceived by undergraduate students of Prince Abubakar Audu University, Anyigba, Kogi State, Nigeria. The study was anchored on the Technology Acceptance Model and Cognitive Load Theory. A mixed-methods, descriptive survey design was adopted, and a multi-stage sampling technique was used to select 380 undergraduates from the Faculties of Management Sciences, Social Sciences and Natural Sciences, with the sample size determined using Krejcie and Morgan's formula. Primary data were obtained through structured questionnaires and in-depth interviews, while secondary data were drawn from journals, textbooks and other relevant publications. Quantitative data were analysed using frequencies, percentages, mean scores, chi-square and independent samples t-test, while qualitative data from the interviews were analysed thematically. Findings revealed a high prevalence of AI usage among undergraduates, with ChatGPT the most widely used tool, followed by Meta AI, Google Gemini, Grammarly, Microsoft Copilot, QuillBot and Photomath. Students reported using these tools mainly to generate ideas, summarise lecture notes, improve writing, solve academic problems and prepare for examinations. Hypothesis testing revealed a statistically significant relationship between the prevalence of AI usage and academic stress reduction (χ² = 43.805, df = 1, p < .001) and between patterns of AI usage and academic stress reduction (χ² = 96.755, df = 1, p < .001), while no significant difference was found in the reduction of academic stress between male and female undergraduates (t(378) = -0.542, p = .588). The study concluded that artificial intelligence has become an important academic resource that contributes meaningfully to reducing academic stress among undergraduates when used responsibly. It recommended that university management should organise regular AI training programmes, strengthen digital infrastructure and develop clear policies guiding the ethical and effective use of artificial intelligence among students.

ABSTRACT The rapid development of Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), cloud computing, big data analytics, blockchain and digital payment technologies is transforming the structure and functioning of modern commerce. The financial services sector is one of the most technology-intensive sectors, where digital transformation has changed traditional banking, payment systems, lending, investment management, insurance and customer relationship management. Artificial Intelligence has emerged as a particularly important technology because of its ability to analyse large volumes of structured and unstructured data, identify patterns, automate decisions and provide personalised services.This chapter examines the role of Artificial Intelligence in transforming financial services and creating emerging business models. It discusses major applications of AI in banking and finance, including fraud detection, credit assessment, customer service, personalised financial products, risk management, regulatory compliance, investment management and digital payments. The chapter also examines emerging models such as AI-powered banking, embedded finance, Banking-as-a-Service, FinTech platforms, intelligent digital lending and AI-enabled financial ecosystems. At the same time, the adoption of AI introduces challenges related to data privacy, cybersecurity, algorithmic bias, explainability, model risk, technological dependency and regulatory compliance. The chapter proposes a responsible AI adoption framework based on governance, data quality, transparency, human oversight, cybersecurity and continuous monitoring. The discussion is particularly relevant to emerging markets such as India, where digital public infrastructure and FinTech innovation are rapidly changing the financial ecosystem.

The tourism and hospitality sector is experiencing a rapid digital transformation driven by artificial intelligence (AI), data analytics, mobile technologies, automation, and increasingly connected service environments. These technologies are changing how travellers search for information, select accommodation, communicate with service providers, and evaluate their experiences. At the same time, hotels and tourism enterprises are using digital tools to improve operational efficiency, personalise services, support employees, and make decisions based on data. This article examines the main opportunities and challenges associated with AI and digital transformation in tourism and hospitality, with particular attention to service quality and the role of human employees. The paper uses a narrative review of recent international research and policy literature. The analysis indicates that AI can support customer communication, demand forecasting, recommendation systems, revenue management, multilingual assistance, and routine operational tasks. However, successful digital transformation depends not only on technology but also on employee skills, data governance, privacy protection, service design, and the preservation of meaningful human interaction. The article argues that technology should be implemented as a tool for strengthening hospitality rather than as a substitute for hospitality itself. The findings are relevant to hospitality managers, tourism educators, students, and policymakers seeking to prepare the sector for a more digital and data-informed future.

ABSTRACT: The use of the nasal cavity is no longer just for local delivery but is emerging as a platform for local, systemic, vaccine and central nervous system delivery. Its clinical and formulation potential is due to the rapid absorption trough the high vascularized mucosal, the lack of gastrointestinal degradation and the first – pass effect in the liver and the potential for direct penetration into the brain via the olfactory and trigeminal pathways. Concurrently, nasal delivery is tightly connected with formulation, device, administration, anatomical and physiological parameters are involved in the system, the traditional trial-and-error development is challenging. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are data-driven methods that can uncover relationships between these variables and helps predict, optimize and design on an individual basis, which are described in the source review. This review summarizes the key concepts presented in the original article, including overview of the principles of nasal delivery, mechanisms of absorption, advantages and limitations, concept of AI/ML and deep learning, applications of AI in formulation and nanocarrier design, nose-to-brain delivery, dataset development and pre-processing, feature engineering, model training and validation, deposition factors associated with the device, performance metrics, deposition prediction using AI/ML, advanced modelling of nano pharmaceutical, AI -enabled digital twins, deposition in the olfactory region, regional deposition modelling, challenges, the future prospects stress is laid on the emitted dose volume, spray pattern, plume geometry, droplet size, emission velocity, and the properties of the formulation, nasal anatomy and breathing conditions as interconnected factors affecting deposition. It also emphasizes the examples from the source article that include a 335-product formulation dataset, machine learning-based excipient prediction, 3D nasal casts solid lipid nanoparticle nasal sprays, and CFD connected deposition modelling. Overall, the evidence from source helps to establish AL/ML as an enabling technology and not a replacement for pharmaceutical experimentation. Before wide clinical and industrial implementation, standardized datasets, strong internal and external validation, explainable models, mechanistic integration and experimental/clinical verification are fundamental. Keywords: artificial intelligence; Machine learning; Nasal drug delivery; Nose-to-brain delivery; Formulation optimization; Olfactory region deposition

Aims: This critical review examines how artificial intelligence (AI) and post-quantum cryptography (PQC) can be combined to strengthen cybersecurity in healthcare information systems, with an emphasis on the Internet of Medical Things (IoMT), clinical data platforms, zero-trust access control and cryptographic migration. Study Design: The review uses a structured literature-search and evidence-mapping approach. It emphasises peer-reviewed sources in computer science, cybersecurity, healthcare informatics and cryptography, as well as authoritative standards. Methodology: Evidence was organised into healthcare/IoMT cybersecurity, AI-enabled detection and response, PQC and migration, and integrated security architecture. NIST, FDA and IETF material was used to distinguish finalised standards from emerging work. Studies were compared by security function, deployment layer, resource overhead, interoperability, clinical risk and empirical validation. Results: AI and PQC address different but complementary requirements. AI supports anomaly detection, behavioural analytics, alert prioritisation and migration assistance, but is exposed to evasion, poisoning, drift and explainability problems. NIST FIPS 203, FIPS 204 and FIPS 205 provide finalised standards for ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA. Major deployment barriers include constrained devices, larger keys and signatures, legacy dependencies, interoperability, implementation leakage, regulation and limited real-world validation. A five-layer reference architecture and a phased migration architecture are proposed. Conclusion: Healthcare organisations should begin cryptographic discovery and risk-based PQC migration while strengthening AI security controls. Future work should prioritise hardware-aware PQC benchmarks, adversarially robust AI, clinically safe automated responses, cryptographic agility and multi-site validation.

documents.abstract: AI is one of the essential technological developments that have taken place in English Language Teaching (ELT). New opportunities for language learning are presented by AI tools like ChatGPT, intelligent tutoring systems, speech-recognition software and automated writing tools. They are able to facilitate personalised learning, communication practice, writing development, vocabulary building, and immediate feedback. Meanwhile, AI presents issues of academic honesty, inaccuracy, privacy, inequity and reliance. Hence, AI needs to be used as an assistant pedagogical tool and not as a replacement of teachers. This article explores the impact of AI in ELT, considers its impact on language abilities, and discusses the shifting nature of the teacher's role, its challenges and future possibilities. It proposes that AI can be a valuable tool in the realm of effective English language education when used in a balanced, ethical, and human-centred manner.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence has recently gained popularity across different medical fields to aid in the detection of diseases based on pathology samples or medical imaging findings. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a key assessment tool for patients with temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE). The role of machine learning and artificial intelligence to increase detection of brain abnormalities in TLE remains inconclusive. We used support vector machine (SV) and deep learning (DL) models based on region of interest (ROI-based) structural (n = 336) and diffusion (n = 863) brain MRI data from patients with TLE with ("lesional") and without ("non-lesional") radiographic features suggestive of underlying hippocampal sclerosis from the multinational (multi-center) ENIGMA-Epilepsy consortium. Our data showed that models to identify TLE performed better or similar (68-75%) compared to models to lateralize the side of TLE (56-73%, except structural-based) based on diffusion data with the opposite pattern seen for structural data (67-75% to diagnose vs. 83% to lateralize). In other aspects, structural and diffusion-based models showed similar classification accuracies. Our classification models for patients with hippocampal sclerosis were more accurate (68-76%) than models that stratified non-lesional patients (53-62%). Overall, SV and DL models performed similarly with several instances in which SV mildly outperformed DL. We discuss the relative performance of these models with ROI-level data and the implications for future applications of machine learning and artificial intelligence in epilepsy care.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative technology with significant potential to advance sustainable development across environmental, social, and economic dimensions. This systematic review synthesizes existing research on the applications, opportunities, and challenges of AI in promoting sustainability. The review examines studies published across multiple disciplines, highlighting how AI-driven technologies contribute to environmental protection through climate change mitigation, energy optimization, waste management, biodiversity conservation, and smart resource utilization. In the social dimension, AI supports improvements in healthcare, education, public safety, social inclusion, and disaster response by enabling data-driven decision-making and enhancing service accessibility. Economically, AI fosters sustainable growth by increasing productivity, optimizing supply chains, encouraging innovation, and facilitating the transition toward circular and digital economies. Despite these promising contributions, the review also identifies several critical challenges associated with AI adoption, including algorithmic bias, data privacy concerns, cybersecurity risks, high energy consumption of AI models, unequal access to AI technologies, and ethical and regulatory issues. These limitations may hinder the achievement of sustainability goals if not addressed through responsible AI governance and inclusive policy frameworks. The findings emphasize that the successful integration of AI into sustainability initiatives requires interdisciplinary collaboration among researchers, policymakers, industry stakeholders, and civil society. Furthermore, transparent AI systems, ethical standards, and environmentally efficient computing infrastructures are essential to maximizing AI's positive impact while minimizing unintended consequences. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the current state of knowledge, identifies research gaps, and proposes future directions for developing trustworthy and sustainable AI solutions aligned with global sustainability objectives. Overall, AI represents a powerful enabler of sustainable development, provided that its implementation is guided by ethical principles, robust governance, and long-term environmental and societal considerations.

Thesis. Recent advances in generative AI, learning systems, and automated feedback tools have sparked discussion about the role of AI in education, encompassing technological innovations, pedagogical transformations, and ethical considerations. While educational institutions increasingly experiment with AI-driven tools, the success of these initiatives depends less on technological availability and more on how educators and learners perceive, accept, and intend to use these technologies meaningfully. Concept. The current research presents a conceptual framework for explaining Omani attitudes and intentions about AI adoption in higher education. By combining interdisciplinary literature and including Oman-specific contextual elements, the study seeks to advance theory and lay the groundwork for future empirical research. Results. The suggested framework's central notion is that attitudes toward AI in education serve as a link between essential determinants and intention to use AI. People's readiness to adopt AI into education is ultimately influenced by their overall evaluative attitude Conclusion. Within GCC, Oman presents a particularly important and underexplored context for studying AI in education. Guided by Oman Vision 2040, the country has prioritised education and human capital development as key drivers of sustainable growth. By combining interdisciplinary literature and including Oman-specific contextual elements, the study seeks to advance theory and lay the groundwork for future empirical research.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) represents a paradigm shift in the education sector, offering transformative opportunities for teaching, learning, and educational management. This paper aims to examine the potential benefits and challenges of AI in education, as well as the existing policy and legal frameworks governing its application. An integrative literature review was employed to achieve this objective. Relevant peer-reviewed journal articles and scholarly documents were retrieved primarily from ScienceDirect and Springer and were synthesized using thematic analysis. The review revealed that AI offers significant benefits, including enhanced instructional delivery, personalized learning, and improved administrative efficiency. However, it also presents critical challenges related to data privacy and security, technological capacity and skills limitations, ethical concerns, algorithmic bias, and equity. Furthermore, the review found that while several international and national legal and policy frameworks exist to regulate AI, these frameworks remain fragmented and largely generalized, particularly in addressing the unique needs of the education sector. Therefore, there is a need for collaborative efforts among policymakers, educational leaders, teachers, and other stakeholders to develop a context-responsive AI governance framework that supports the responsible, ethical, and equitable integration of AI in Philippine basic education.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming health care, offering new opportunities to enhance education, clinical care, and system-level integration. Lifestyle medicine (LM), with its emphasis on behavior change and whole-person care is particularly well positioned to benefit from these advances. This perspective provides an overview of emerging and potential applications of AI across the field, including clinician training and self-directed learning, AI-augmented clinical supervision, patient-facing tools for health behavior change, mental health and emotional well-being, real-time access to scientific evidence, clinical reasoning support, and system-level planning to connect with community resources that address social determinants of health. While these tools offer significant promise to improve scalability, consistency, and personalization of care, they also introduce risks related to data privacy, bias, and overreliance on automated recommendations. Acknowledging recent controversies about AI risks and the rapid evolution of this technology, we propose practical guardrails for clinicians and highlight the importance of leadership engagement to ensure that AI development and its use in the field aligns with the principles of LM and whole-person care. Thoughtful integration of AI with human agency that propels critical thinking has the potential to strengthen, rather than diminish, the human-centered foundations of whole-person care.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming medicine, yet AI competencies remain insufficiently integrated into medical curricula, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. This study investigated AI tool use, self-rated proficiency, and attitudes towards AI in medical education, physician roles, and patient care among medical undergraduates at a Sri Lankan medical faculty, including comparisons across year groups and gender. A cross-sectional online survey was conducted among Years 1–5 medical undergraduates at SUSL in May 2025. The questionnaire assessed demographics, AI tool use, self-rated proficiency, and 12 Likert-scale items covering curriculum integration, physician roles, and patient care. Descriptive statistics, Kruskal–Wallis H-tests, Mann–Whitney U-tests, and chi-square tests were used for analysis. A total of 369 responses were analysed. Reported use of AI-based applications was high (99.2%; 366/369). Among respondents reporting AI use ( n = 366), ChatGPT was the most frequently used tool (98.1%), followed by Google Gemini (35.0%), DeepSeek (20.2%), and Microsoft Copilot (6.3%). The main uses of AI were subject-matter reference (89.3%), general information retrieval (73.0%), assignment assistance (50.8%), and writing improvement (39.6%). Self-rated proficiency was highest for ChatGPT, with 92.4% of respondents rating their proficiency as good or higher. Among respondents in the medical information/reference application analysis ( n = 360), 77.5% used Medscape, followed by UpToDate (37.2%) and WebMD/WebMD Symptom Checker (15.3%). Most students agreed that AI could enhance learning in preclinical (85.1%), paraclinical (77.8%), and clinical (68.6%) subjects. After adjustment for multiple comparisons, support for including AI in the medical curriculum differed significantly across year groups (H = 29.00, Holm-adjusted p < 0.001), with higher agreement among some earlier-year groups. Medical undergraduates demonstrated high levels of self-reported AI tool use despite limited formal training. Attitudes toward AI differed for selected items between preclinical and clinical students, although longitudinal change cannot be inferred from these cross-sectional data. These findings support consideration of structured, ethically grounded AI education in undergraduate medical curricula to address students’ educational needs relating to the safe, effective, and responsible use of AI.
